formats_page.hero_text: Technical details and bitstream preservation behavior for each format supported by the client-side engine.

jpg.behavior: Byte-level marker manipulation. APP segments are removed without re-encoding the picture.

png.segments: eXIf, tEXt, zTXt, iTXt (ancillary metadata chunks)
png.behavior: Bitwise chunk filtering drops metadata; image and alpha data stay untouched.

webp.segments: RIFF headers, EXIF and XMP sub-chunks
webp.behavior: The RIFF container is parsed and metadata chunks are removed without touching the image stream.

tiff.segments: IFD0, IFD1, ExifIFD, GPSIFD, IPTC, XMP
tiff.behavior: The image-file directory chain is walked and metadata pointer tags are stripped.

heic.segments: ISOBMFF box structure, meta boxes, exif items
heic.behavior: HEIC/HEIF is re-encoded to a clean JPEG at maximum quality because browsers cannot strip HEIC in place.

how_it_works_page.steps_title: 5 Steps from Loaded File to Sanitized Image

1.title: Select Your Photo
1.text: When you drag and drop or select an image, the browser mounts a read-only pointer to the file. Your original photo on disk is never modified or relocated.

2.title: Scan Metadata
2.text: The parser reads the raw binary bytes and walks the file headers, recognizing JPEG markers, PNG chunk types, and HEIC/TIFF box structures to build a complete tag inventory.

3.title: Review Metadata
3.text: Detected data is grouped into clear categories: GPS coordinates, device serial numbers, timestamps, and camera settings. You get full transparency about what is hiding in your file.

4.title: Remove Metadata
4.text: Instead of re-rendering through a canvas, the engine excises only the metadata bytes. The original pixel data stays untouched, so there is no quality loss.

5.title: Download Clean Image
5.text: The sanitized binary is wrapped into an in-memory blob and linked to an instant download. For batches, the cleaned files are packed into a ZIP archive directly in your browser.

how_it_works_page.compare_intro: Unlike converters that re-compress images into new JPEGs, this tool removes unwanted segments while preserving your photography exactly as captured.
how_it_works_page.remove_intro: Identifying tracking vectors, camera serial numbers, and private exposure markers are isolated and removed from the header stream.

remove_items.2: Device identifiers & serial numbers — unique body serials, lens IDs, and camera model codes.
remove_items.3: Exact timestamps & sub-second offsets — original creation dates and timezone signatures.
remove_items.4: Embedded thumbnails & MakerNotes — old preview images cached inside the EXIF block.
remove_items.5: Software & copyright entries — editing history, artist tags, and application names.

how_it_works_page.keep_intro: Your photo's visual fidelity is never modified. Because nothing is re-encoded, there is zero generational quality degradation.

keep_items.1: Full native resolution — every pixel width and height stays identical.
keep_items.2: Lossless pixel data — no re-compression artifacts, color shift, or bit-depth reduction.
keep_items.3: Color profile — sRGB, Adobe RGB, or Display P3 matrices remain calibrated.
keep_items.4: Transparency — PNG or WebP transparent backgrounds remain crisp.
keep_items.5: Image stream — the scan data containing the visuals stays bit-for-bit untouched.

how_it_works_page.lossless_text: Many online scrubbers load images into an HTML canvas and re-export them, degrading detail. Our approach operates purely at the binary container layer.

1.question: What is EXIF data?
1.answer: EXIF stands for Exchangeable Image File Format. It is a standard that stores technical information in photos â€“ such as the camera model, lens, exposure settings, and the date the photo was taken.

2.question: Can EXIF data be seen by other people?
2.answer: Yes. When you share the original file, recipients can read its EXIF data with any photo viewer, EXIF viewer, or online tool. That's why it's safer to remove it before sharing.

3.question: Does removing EXIF data affect the photo?
3.answer: No. The visible image is unchanged. Only the hidden metadata section is removed, so the photo looks and functions exactly as before.

remove-gps-data.subtitle: Delete the exact GPS coordinates that cameras and phones store in your photos.
remove-gps-data.intro: Most smartphones and many cameras save the exact GPS coordinates of the place where a photo was taken. Anyone who receives the original file can read that location â€“ right down to the street. With our free GPS remover you delete these coordinates in seconds, completely in your browser and without uploading the photo anywhere.

1.question: Do all photos contain GPS data?
1.answer: No. GPS coordinates are only stored when the camera or smartphone had location services enabled when the photo was taken. When in doubt, check your photo â€“ our viewer shows you what's hidden inside.

2.answer: Yes. Many photo programs let you save coordinates into an image manually. Removing them is the reliable way to keep your locations private.

3.question: Is removing GPS data enough for privacy?
3.answer: Usually not. Photos also contain other metadata such as your camera model or timestamps. For full privacy, remove all metadata â€“ our photo metadata remover does this in one step.

1.question: What is a HEIC file?
1.answer: HEIC (High Efficiency Image Coding) is a modern image format used by Apple. It stores photos with better compression than JPG but contains the same kind of hidden metadata.

2.question: Does removing metadata from HEIC reduce quality?
2.answer: HEIC is re-encoded to JPEG during processing, so the clean output is a lossy JPEG (quality 0.92). The image is rebuilt from pixels with all metadata stripped. For a format-preserving, lossless result, use JPG or PNG files instead.

3.question: Are HEIC photos shared as HEIC?
3.answer: Not always. Many apps convert HEIC to JPG when you share. Both formats contain metadata, so strip it before sending â€“ regardless of the output format.

q1.question: What is photo metadata?
q1.answer: Photo metadata is hidden header information stored inside an image file. Every time you capture a picture, the device automatically stamps the file with non-visual data: device identifiers, capture timestamps, camera settings, and often GPS coordinates.

q2.question: What is EXIF?
q2.answer: EXIF (Exchangeable Image File Format) is the standard that digital cameras use to write operational tags into files like JPEG and TIFF. Alongside EXIF, images often carry IPTC data (captions and copyright) and XMP data (Adobe's extensible metadata).

q3.question: Can photos contain my home GPS coordinates?
q3.answer: Yes. If location permissions are enabled on your camera app, GPS satellites inject latitude, longitude, and elevation into the file. Anyone who downloads the original file can map your exact location.

q4.question: Does Photo Metadata Remover upload my photos to a server?
q4.answer: Never. Everything runs inside your browser. You can turn off your internet connection after the page loads and the tool continues to work — that is the clearest proof that nothing is sent anywhere.

q5.question: How does browser-based processing work?
q5.answer: When you drop a file, the browser reads it into memory. The parser locates the metadata markers, you review what was found, and only the sensitive bytes are removed. The result is a new file you download. Everything happens in your browser tab.

q6.question: Can I inspect metadata before removing it?
q6.answer: Yes. The tool scans each photo and lists the privacy-sensitive fields it found — GPS, device, timestamps, software — so you can review exactly what will be stripped before you download the clean file.

q7.question: What happens if my image has no metadata?
q7.answer: The scan reports that no privacy metadata was found, and you can use the file as-is. Nothing is modified in that case.

q8.question: Which formats are supported?
q8.answer: JPEG/JPG, PNG, WebP, TIFF, and HEIC/HEIF. Each format is processed according to how it actually stores metadata — see the Supported Formats page for details.

q9.question: Does removing metadata change image quality?
q9.answer: No. For JPG, PNG, WebP, and TIFF the pixels are never re-encoded — only the metadata blocks are removed, so quality is preserved bit-for-bit.

q10.question: What happens with HEIC/HEIF files?
q10.answer: Apple devices store photos in HEIC/HEIF. Because browsers cannot strip metadata inside HEIC in place, the tool re-encodes those photos to a clean JPEG at maximum quality with all metadata removed.

q11.question: Can I process multiple images at once?
q11.answer: Yes. Drop several files at once, remove metadata from all of them, and download them individually or as a single ZIP archive — all generated locally in your browser.

q13.question: Can I verify that nothing is uploaded?
q13.answer: Absolutely. Open your browser's developer tools, switch to the Network tab, and use the tool. You will see zero outbound requests while a photo is processed — the bytes never leave your device.

home_seo.intro: Every photo carries hidden data that most image viewers never show you: GPS coordinates of where you stood, the exact camera and lens, the moment it was taken, and the software that last touched the file. A photo metadata remover strips that layer so the picture travels without the trail behind it.

sections.h2: What Is a Photo Metadata Remover?

blocks.text: Photo metadata is descriptive information stored inside an image file rather than inside the visible picture. Cameras and phones write it automatically, in three main families: EXIF (capture date and time, camera make and model, lens and exposure settings, often GPS coordinates), IPTC (captions, keywords, credits) and XMP (editing history).

None of this is visible when you look at the photo, which is why it matters: a family photo in a listing can still carry the coordinates of your home, and a serial number can tie two unrelated photos to the same device.

A metadata remover reads those fields, shows you which it found, and removes the supported ones while leaving the picture untouched. Removal happens at file level, so the image is not recompressed — which matters with originals you cannot afford to degrade. Our [guide to checking photo metadata](blog_check) walks through the common fields.

sections.h2: Remove Photo Metadata Online Without Uploading Your Photos

blocks.text: Online usually implies a server: you send a photo, it is processed, it comes back. That is how most hosted cleaners work, and it creates an awkward problem — the file carrying your location is copied onto hardware you do not control.

This photo metadata remover online takes a different approach. Your browser reads the file directly from your device, parses the metadata locally and hands back a clean copy as a download. Nothing is transmitted — open your browser network panel while it runs and you will see no request carrying your image.
The five-step workflow

items: Upload or drop a photo, or queue several as a batch.
Scan. The browser parses the file and lists detected fields.
Remove. Supported metadata is stripped, image data preserved.
Verify. The output is re-read before being shown as clean.
Download. Save the image, or the batch as a ZIP.

blocks.text: Because everything runs locally, the same tool works on a phone or a desktop alike. Our [privacy page](privacy) covers the architecture, the [security page](security) the threat model.

sections.h2: What Metadata Can Be Removed From a Photo?

blocks.text: The removable fields depend on the format and on what the writing device recorded. Across the formats we handle:

items: GPS and location data — coordinates, altitude and location tags.
Camera make and model, serial numbers, device identifiers.
Lens information, including name, focal length and aperture.
Capture date and time, plus original and digitised timestamps.
Author and creator fields, copyright, IPTC captions and keywords.
Software and editing information, including XMP history.
Comments and other embedded text such as UserComment.

blocks.text: The visible picture is never touched. For JPEG, PNG, WebP and TIFF the image data is preserved rather than re-encoded, so you do not trade privacy for quality. HEIC is the one format browsers cannot edit in place, so those files are decoded and written back as a clean JPEG — see the [supported formats page](formats). A file only exposes what was written to it: a photo from a messaging app has usually been stripped by the platform already.

sections.h2: Photo Metadata Remover for Android, iPhone and Windows

blocks.text: This is a browser-based tool rather than an installable application: nothing to download, nothing to update, no permission prompts. Any device with a current browser can run it.
Using it on an Android phone

Looking for a photo metadata remover Android app? You can use this browser-based tool directly from an Android browser without installing a separate application. Open the page in Chrome, tap the upload area, choose a photo from your gallery and download the cleaned file.
Using it on an iPhone

If you need an iPhone photo metadata remover, open the tool in your mobile browser and process your image directly on your device. Safari is supported, and HEIC photos from the default camera app come back as clean JPEGs — the [iPhone guide](blog_iphone) explains why.
Using it on Windows and macOS

For Windows users, the online photo metadata remover works directly in a modern desktop browser such as Edge, Chrome or Firefox — no installer and no separate Windows application. The same applies on macOS. Because the tool is not tied to a device, the photo metadata remover app you use is simply your browser.

sections.h2: Photo Metadata Viewer Before You Remove Metadata

blocks.text: Looking before you delete is worthwhile. The scan step doubles as a photo metadata viewer: it lists the fields it found before anything changes, so you can see whether a file carries GPS coordinates, which camera wrote it, or whether it was already cleaned elsewhere.

If a photo arrives from someone else, seeing the metadata online tells you when and where it was taken. If you publish your own work, it confirms no coordinates or serial numbers go out with it. Because scan and removal share one parser, there is no gap between the [preview and the result](formats).

sections.h2: AI Photo Metadata Remover: What Does That Mean?

blocks.text: Some people search for an AI photo metadata remover when they want an automated way to identify and remove hidden image information. This tool focuses on local browser-based metadata scanning and removal rather than requiring an AI service or uploading your photo.

That is a deliberate choice, not a missing feature. Metadata sits in documented structures, so a deterministic parser removes exactly what it found — no guesswork, no third-party dependency, and it works offline once loaded. [What EXIF data is](guide_exif) and [how GPS tags reveal location](guide_gps) are the best starting points.

sections.h2: Why Remove Metadata From Photos Before Sharing?

blocks.text: Most people only think about metadata after something has leaked. Cleaning a photo first is cheaper than cleaning up afterwards.

items: Social media. Not every platform strips GPS data on upload.
Marketplaces and listings. Seller photos can reveal where you live.
Forums and message boards. Long-lived threads are searchable and archived.
Messaging apps. Images shared as files keep their metadata.
Email attachments. The original is often forwarded untouched.
Websites and portfolios. Full-resolution originals go up uncleaned.
Professional work. Shared drafts can expose dates and studio details.

blocks.text: None of this is about hiding that you took a photograph — it is about deciding which incidental details travel with it. Our [social media guide](guide_social) looks at how platforms handle uploads.

sections.h2: How to Remove Metadata From a Photo

blocks.text: The process takes under a minute. It suits beginners and technical users equally, because every step reports what it did rather than asking you to trust it.

items: Select or drop a photo. Multiple files can be queued at once.
Let the browser scan the file. Parsing happens locally.
Review the detected metadata, particularly GPS coordinates.
Remove the supported metadata. Image data stays intact.
Verify the cleaned output. It is only presented as clean if it is.
Download the clean image and keep your original somewhere private.

blocks.text: For a large set, run it as a batch and download the ZIP. A file with no removable metadata simply reports nothing to strip.
